name: Ding white ware
summary: Thin ivory-white porcelain of the Northern Song court. The potters of Ding carve or mould fine plant designs under a clear glaze and fire the bowls rim down, so they bind the bare rim with metal.

philosophy.core_thesis: A white body and a clear ivory glaze are enough: the beauty is the thin wall, the carved line and the quiet tone.
design_principles: Throw the bowl with a wall 2 to 3 mm thick and turn it on the outside to a fine profile.
Cut the design in the leather-hard body with a comb or a knife, in lines 1 to 2 mm wide.
Press a moulded design of peony, lotus or fish into the inside of a dish for a sharp relief.
Cover the piece in a clear glaze with a trace of iron, so that it fires to an ivory white.
Stack the bowl rim down on a ring support to fire many pieces in one kiln.
Leave the rim bare after firing and bind it with a band of silver or copper.
Allow a few tear-like runs of glaze on the outside; they are a mark of the kiln.
anti_patterns: A blue-white glaze like the ware of Jingdezhen
Painted colour under or over the glaze
A thick wall with a heavy foot
Bright enamel or gilt panels across the surface

form.shape: Conical and flaring bowls, small dishes with a lobed rim, flat plates and small cups on a low foot.
form.profile: A straight, open cone, or a shallow dish with a wide mouth; the line from foot to rim has no break.
form.foot_and_rim: A narrow, neat foot ring with a bare unglazed rim, which a band of metal often covers; the lobed rim has 6 or 8 points.
form.proportion: Bowl diameter 12 to 25 cm, height 5 to 9 cm, and a wall 2 to 3 mm thick at the rim.
rules: Keep one clean curve from the foot to the mouth.
Carve or mould the decoration only on the inside, in one band.
Leave the rim bare, because the bowl fires upside down.

bodies.rule: Use a fine white kaolin body that fires dense and nearly translucent. Do not use a coloured stoneware: the glaze needs a white ground.

methods: throwing thin walls on the wheel
press moulding in a fired clay mould
metal banding of the bare rim
forming.joins: Handles are rare; a metal band covers the bare rim after the firing.
forming.details: Fine comb lines under the glaze, a ring of bare rim, and small tear-like runs of glaze on the outside.

glaze.pattern: Peony and lotus scrolls, ducks, fish, and wild geese on a water ground, cut or moulded in one band inside the bowl.
glaze.gloss: Soft gloss, about 50 to 70 GU, with a warm ivory tone.
glaze.wear: The glaze stays smooth; the metal band on the rim wears or leaves a green stain.

palette.strategy: One ivory white, a warm cream where the glaze is thick, and a brown trace at the tear runs.

firing.kiln: A kiln that burns wood and, from the 11th century, coal; the bowls stand rim down on ring supports in saggars.
processes: biscuit firing at a low heat
stacking rim down on ring supports
binding the bare rim with metal
firing.scale: The kilns of Quyang supplied the court and the market in the north of China.
firing.signs: A bare ring at the rim, tear-like runs on the outside, and fine comb lines that show through the glaze.

lineage.root: Song potters at Quyang made the first ivory-white porcelain in this data; no earlier style here leads to it.

emotion.target_response: A hushed, refined calm: the viewer sees a thin white bowl and a single carved flower, and speaks softly.

use_cases: a museum label on Song white ware
a minimal plating prompt for a tasting menu

the brief needs a dense, heavy stoneware
the brief wants an industrial printed pattern

modifiers.how: Keep the porcelain body and add cobalt painting under the glaze in panels.
Change to a dark iron-rich stoneware with a thick glaze that runs, and keep the conical bowl.

wall_thickness.note: The thin wall is the mark of the style.
